That is why Lambda is so economical for **intermittent or spiky** work: an EC2 instance would be billed for all the idle time in between.
## Where it may not
If a service is busy all the time, there is little idle time to save. A rightsized EC2 fleet running near full use, especially with a Savings Plan, can then cost less per request than paying Lambda's per-request and per-millisecond charges for the same constant load.
## How to decide
- Estimate both options with the **AWS Pricing Calculator** using real request counts, durations and memory sizes.
- Include operations in the total: Lambda removes server patching and scaling work, which has value of its own.
- Compute Savings Plans can apply to Lambda as well as to EC2.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Compare with real usage (correct):** Lambda's advantage is not paying for idle time. A service that is busy around the clock has little idle time, so Lambda may cost more, and only an estimate with actual traffic shows which is cheaper.
- ✗ **B. Always cheaper:** removing idle cost helps only when there is idle time. For constant heavy load, per-request and per-duration charges can exceed the cost of busy, rightsized instances.
- ✗ **C. Same price as EC2:** the two services use different pricing models (per request and duration versus per instance running time), so the cost of the same workload usually differs.
- ✗ **D. One-minute minimum:** Lambda bills duration in 1 ms increments, not per minute. The real question is the usage pattern, not a minimum charge.

## Key idea
Serverless pay-per-use pricing saves the most for idle-heavy workloads; for steady, high utilization, compare Lambda and EC2 with real usage before moving.
Q006171:
## Undifferentiated heavy lifting
Running software yourself on EC2 means installing it, patching the OS and application, planning capacity, building high availability and handling failures. This work is necessary but does not make the company's products better. AWS calls it **undifferentiated heavy lifting**.
## What managed services change economically
Managed services such as Amazon RDS, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon S3, Amazon SQS or AWS Lambda:
- remove routine operational tasks, so staff time costs fall or move to more valuable work;
- include scaling and availability features (for example DynamoDB scales throughput, S3 stores data across multiple AZs), so the company does not build and pay for spare capacity and standby systems itself.
## What does not change
Managed services still charge for usage. The customer still manages access with IAM and protects its data, and it still owns compliance for its own workloads under the shared responsibility model.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Compliance moves to AWS:** AWS provides compliance reports for its infrastructure, but the company remains responsible for compliance of its own data, configurations and processes.
- ✗ **B. No access control needed:** the customer still grants and restricts access with IAM policies and resource settings. Security in the cloud remains the customer's job.
- ✗ **C. Free with EC2:** managed services have their own usage-based pricing. Owning EC2 instances does not make any other service free.
- ✓ **D. Lower operational overhead (correct):** AWS performs the provisioning, patching and hardware upkeep for the managed service, so the company spends less staff time on routine operations.
- ✓ **E. Built-in scaling and availability (correct):** managed services include scaling and redundancy, so the company avoids paying for and maintaining its own extra capacity and failover systems.

## Key idea
Managed services reduce cost by cutting operational work and by including scaling and availability the customer would otherwise build itself.
Q006172:
## Cloud economics is more than a smaller bill
AWS describes the value of moving to the cloud along several dimensions (the AWS Cloud Value Framework):
- **Cost savings**: lower infrastructure spending, the part most business cases start with.
- **Staff productivity**: less time on undifferentiated tasks such as hardware upkeep and patching, so people work on higher-value projects.
- **Operational resilience**: better availability and security, which means fewer and shorter outages and less lost revenue.
- **Business agility**: faster experiments and releases, so new products reach customers sooner.
## Why it matters
A business case that counts only infrastructure savings may undervalue the move, or even make it look unattractive when infrastructure costs are similar. Measuring productivity, resilience and agility gives a complete picture.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Hardware resale value only:** resale may help a little, but it is a small one-time item and says nothing about the ongoing value of the cloud.
- ✓ **B. Productivity, resilience and agility (correct):** these are the value dimensions beyond infrastructure savings. Time freed from routine work, fewer outages and faster releases all carry business value that a cost-only case ignores.
- ✗ **C. Managed service prices only:** managed services can have higher unit prices, but they also reduce staff effort. Counting only their price gives a one-sided view.
- ✗ **D. Migration cost only:** migration costs belong in the case, but treating infrastructure savings as the only long-term value leaves out productivity, resilience and agility.

## Key idea
A complete cloud business case adds staff productivity, operational resilience and business agility to the infrastructure cost savings.
Q006173:
## Storage outlives instances
An EC2 instance and its Amazon EBS volumes are separate resources:
- The root volume created at launch is usually set to **delete on termination**.
- Additional data volumes are often set **not** to delete on termination, so terminating the instance leaves them behind as **unattached (available) volumes**.
- **Snapshots** taken for backup stay until someone deletes them.
EBS volumes are billed for their **provisioned size per month**, whether attached or not, and snapshots are billed for the data they store.
## Finding and removing the waste
- In the EC2 console, filter volumes by state `available` to find unattached ones.
- Review old snapshots and delete those no longer needed (or manage them with Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager).
- AWS Trusted Advisor and AWS Compute Optimizer can flag idle or underused volumes.
Cleaning up orphaned resources is a basic cloud cost practice: on AWS you pay for what you provision, even if nothing uses it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Leftover snapshots (correct):** backup snapshots are independent of the instances and volumes they came from, so they stay and are billed for their stored data until deleted.
- ✗ **B. Fixed EBS account fee:** EBS has no account-level fixed fee. Charges come from resources that still exist, such as volumes (with any provisioned performance) and snapshots.
- ✗ **C. Hidden 90-day copy:** AWS does not keep and bill a hidden copy of terminated instances' disks. Data remains only in volumes and snapshots the customer still has (deleted snapshots are kept in the Recycle Bin only if the customer created a retention rule).
- ✗ **D. Extra month of compute:** EC2 compute charges stop when an instance is terminated. AWS does not add a month of compute, and it would not appear as an EBS charge.
- ✓ **E. Unattached data volumes (correct):** volumes not set to delete on termination survive the instance and keep being billed for their provisioned size until someone deletes them.

## Key idea
After terminating instances, delete unattached EBS volumes and unneeded snapshots, because provisioned storage is billed even when nothing uses it.
Q006174:
## Licensing is part of cloud economics
Commercial database engines often charge license and support fees per core or per server. These can be a large share of a database's total cost. Moving to the cloud gives a chance to change engines.
## Open source compatible engines
**Amazon Aurora** offers MySQL-compatible and PostgreSQL-compatible editions. Customers pay for the database instances or capacity, storage and I/O, with no separate engine license fee. Tools such as AWS Database Migration Service and AWS DMS Schema Conversion help convert schemas and code from commercial engines.
## Trade-off
Changing engines is a **replatform or refactor** step: SQL code, stored procedures and application queries may need changes. The licensing savings must be weighed against that migration effort.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Database files in Glacier:** Glacier storage classes are for archives with retrieval delays. A live database engine cannot run its tables from archive storage.
- ✗ **B. Cheaper Region:** compute prices change slightly, while the license fees, the cost the company wants to cut, remain unchanged.
- ✓ **C. Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible (correct):** moving to an engine based on open source removes the commercial license fee entirely. The company pays for Aurora usage only, which directly lowers long-term licensing cost.
- ✗ **D. Bigger instance, same engine:** fewer servers may help a little, but commercial engines are commonly licensed per core, so a bigger instance can need just as many licenses or more.

## Key idea
Switching from a commercial database engine to an open source compatible engine such as Aurora PostgreSQL removes license fees, at the cost of some migration work.
Q006175:
## Per-core licensing on the cloud
Many commercial products are licensed per CPU core or per vCPU. Large EC2 instance types have many vCPUs, so a workload that needs a lot of **memory** but little **CPU** can end up paying for licenses on cores it hardly uses.
## Optimize CPUs
Amazon EC2 lets customers **optimize CPU options** for supported instance types, usually when the instance is launched:
- set a **custom number of CPU cores** lower than the default;
- set **threads per core** to 1 to turn off simultaneous multithreading.
The instance keeps the same memory, but exposes fewer vCPUs. The EC2 price stays the same; the saving comes from the BYOL license count. AWS presents this specifically as a way to reduce per-core software licensing costs.
## Related tools
- AWS License Manager tracks license usage against the rules.
- Dedicated Hosts give visibility into physical sockets and cores for socket-based licenses.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Elastic IP addresses:** a static public IP address has nothing to do with per-core licensing, and licenses tied to cores are not moved to an address.
- ✗ **B. Hibernation:** hibernation stops the instance and saves memory to disk. When it runs, all of its cores are active and counted.
- ✓ **C. Optimize CPUs (correct):** the instance keeps its large memory but runs with fewer active cores or threads, so the per-core BYOL license covers fewer cores and costs less.
- ✗ **D. Detailed monitoring:** more frequent CloudWatch metrics do not change how a software vendor counts licensed cores. The cores still exist and are counted.

## Key idea
When per-core licenses dominate cost, use EC2 Optimize CPUs to run a large-memory instance with fewer licensed cores.
Q006176:
## Price performance
Price performance means how much work you get for each dollar. Two instances with the same hourly price can deliver very different amounts of work, so choosing a better-suited instance family is one form of cost optimization.
## AWS Graviton
**AWS Graviton** processors are Arm-based chips designed by AWS. Graviton instance families (for example `m7g`, `c7g`, `r7g`) are generally priced lower than comparable x86 instances and often deliver better price performance for workloads such as web services, containers and many databases.
- Interpreted or JIT-compiled languages such as Java, Python and Node.js usually run with little or no code change.
- Compiled native code and some third-party software need an Arm build.
- Testing is still needed, so the move is usually tried on one service first.
## Fit with the economics
This optimization lowers cost per request without a new commitment, and it combines with existing Savings Plans: Compute Savings Plans apply to Graviton instances too.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Dedicated Instances:** single-tenant hardware costs more, not less, than default shared tenancy. It is chosen for isolation or licensing needs, not price performance.
- ✗ **B. Outposts on premises:** Outposts brings AWS infrastructure to a customer site for latency or local data needs. It is not a cheaper way to run web services that already run well in a Region.
- ✗ **C. Largest instance size:** cost scales with size, and an oversized instance wastes capacity. The largest size is not automatically the cheapest per request.
- ✓ **D. Graviton-based instances (correct):** Java runs on the JVM, so the services usually move to Arm with little change, and Graviton families commonly provide more work per dollar than comparable x86 instances.

## Key idea
For workloads that can run on Arm, AWS Graviton-based instances are a common way to improve price performance with little or no code change.
Q006177:
## How EBS is billed
Amazon EBS volumes are billed for the **provisioned size** per GB-month, and some types also for provisioned performance. Choosing the right volume type is a simple, ongoing cost lever.
## gp2 versus gp3
- **gp2** (older General Purpose SSD): performance is tied to size, about 3 IOPS per GB with bursting for small volumes. To get more IOPS, teams often had to buy more GB than they needed.
- **gp3** (current General Purpose SSD): a lower price per GB than gp2, with a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size. Extra IOPS and throughput can be provisioned separately from capacity.
With **Elastic Volumes**, a volume's type can be changed while it stays attached and in use, so the move needs no downtime. Very large gp2 volumes may have a baseline above 3,000 IOPS, so check their needs and provision extra gp3 IOPS where required. AWS Compute Optimizer also gives EBS volume recommendations.
## Other types
- **io2** (Provisioned IOPS SSD): for the most demanding databases; costs more.
- **st1 / sc1** (HDD): cheap, throughput-oriented storage for large sequential data; they cannot be boot volumes.
- **Instance store**: temporary disks on the host; data is lost when the instance stops or terminates.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Move to gp3 (correct):** gp3 has a lower price per GB, its baseline performance does not depend on size, and Elastic Volumes changes the type while volumes stay in use, so cost falls without downtime.
- ✗ **B. Cold HDD (sc1):** sc1 is cheap but is designed for infrequently accessed sequential data and cannot be used as a boot volume, so it does not keep the needed performance.
- ✗ **C. Instance store:** instance store is included in some instance types, but it is temporary storage and its data is lost when the instance is stopped or terminated.
- ✗ **D. io2:** Provisioned IOPS volumes are the premium SSD type and cost more than General Purpose volumes. They suit the most demanding databases, not a cost cut.

## Key idea
Changing gp2 EBS volumes to gp3 with Elastic Volumes lowers the price per GB and separates performance from size, without downtime.
Q006178:
## Total cost versus unit cost
In the cloud, spending is supposed to grow with the business. A rising total bill is not bad by itself; it may simply mean more customers. The useful question is whether each unit of business costs more or less than before.
## Unit metrics
A **unit cost** divides cloud spend by a business measure:
- cost per active user or student;
- cost per order or transaction;
- cost per gigabyte processed.
Example: last year the bill was 100,000 for 50,000 students (2.00 per student). This year it is 200,000 for 150,000 students (about 1.33 per student). Total spend doubled, but the cost of serving each student fell by about a third, which shows improving efficiency.
## Tools
Cost allocation tags, AWS Cost Explorer and AWS Cost and Usage Reports provide the cost side; the business system provides the unit count.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Instance count:** fewer instances can mean larger, more expensive ones, and the count says nothing about how much business they support.
- ✓ **B. Unit cost per student (correct):** spend divided by active students shows that each student costs less to serve than before, even though the bill grew, so the CFO can see efficiency rather than raw growth.
- ✗ **C. Savings Plans coverage:** coverage shows how much usage gets a commitment discount. It does not show whether resources are rightsized or whether each student costs less.
- ✗ **D. Total bill alone:** the total grows naturally with a growing customer base. Without relating spend to business volume, it cannot show whether costs are under control.

## Key idea
Judge cloud spending with unit costs, such as spend per customer, because a growing business should see total spend rise while unit cost falls.
Q006179:
## Commit after you optimize
A **Savings Plan** is a commitment to spend a fixed amount per hour (for example 10 USD/hour) on compute for one or three years, in exchange for lower rates. The commitment is paid whether or not the usage is there.
## The right order
1. **Rightsize** first: shrink or change oversized instances (AWS Compute Optimizer helps), and turn off what is not needed.
2. **Measure** the new, lower steady usage.
3. **Commit** with a Savings Plan or Reserved Instances sized to that steady baseline.
If the company commits first, the hourly commitment is based on waste. After rightsizing later, usage falls below the commitment and the company pays for the unused part anyway.
## Example
Current usage costs 20 USD/hour On-Demand; rightsizing would bring it to 12 USD/hour. A plan sized to today's spend leaves a large share of the commitment unused for three years.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Rightsize, then commit (correct):** rightsizing lowers the steady usage first, and a commitment sized to that lower baseline gets the discount without paying for capacity the company will later remove.
- ✗ **B. Stack Reserved Instances on top:** Reserved Instances and Savings Plans do not both discount the same usage hour, and oversized instances still waste money at any rate.
- ✗ **C. Dedicated Hosts first:** Savings Plans are not limited to dedicated hardware. Dedicated Hosts usually cost more and would add to the waste, not reduce it.
- ✗ **D. Commit to current spending:** the discount rate does not improve because instances are oversized. A bigger commitment only locks in payments for waste that rightsizing would remove.

## Key idea
Rightsize resources before buying Savings Plans or Reserved Instances so the commitment matches real, steady usage.
